listsCellByCell.title: Price lists read cell by cell, the way the owner reads them
listsCellByCell.text: A supplier's price list is now read like a sheet: the sizes across the top and each size's price under it; a cell of digits is a price and a name has a letter; «2 inch / 4 inch» in one cell is one size, from a size to a size. Pipe lists name the pipe by its colour (white and grey drainage, green feed), a grey header's right-hand and left-hand codes are two products, and a maker's colour groups are each a price. The rules sit in one reference that every upload opens. Before it went live, every list the shop had uploaded was read by the old reader and the new one, row by row: one maker's catalogue had fallen from 605 lines to 418 and a model number had been glued into a size — both fixed first, so no line the old reader read was lost. The review now opens on four decisions: a small sure change, a first price or a big change, a new product, or a line that needs the owner.

shopContacts.title: One list of the shop's contacts, each with his own consent — off until the owner turns it on
shopContacts.text: A visitor who does not register still gives a name and a mobile somewhere: the WhatsApp message to the shop, a price statement, an order or a showroom pickup, a design request. Each of these now writes one list — one row a mobile, however it was typed, with a trail of where and when he gave it. Under each form sits one tick, «the shop may contact me with offers», empty until he ticks it (Egypt's personal data law asks his consent); it holds until he asks the shop to stop, and a later form left unticked is no «no». The list is the owner's alone: he stops the offers when someone asks, or erases a person with his whole trail. The other services send their part in the same save as the request or the order; the WhatsApp door is limited per visitor. It arrives switched off — nothing is kept and no form asks — until the owner turns it on.

explainProducts.title: The owner tells the program what products are — and it files them by his word
explainProducts.text: A supplier's list brings products the shop never carried, and the catalogue holds products the program reads wrongly. The owner can now explain either: tick a group of a list's new products, or any product of the catalogue (from the products' list or the «understanding the products» page), and say what they are, the word of their names that says so, and the category they belong in — a new one too, made right there. The program first says, saving nothing, what it would learn and which products learn from it; a name too unclear to learn from is placed only this once. His press keeps the word and the rule; every later list reads its new products by them, and the products he explained move through the same move door as any move, after he sees what moves and every code that changes. A lesson that would undo a placement he decided earlier is refused and nothing is kept. Other products of the same kind are only proposed to him, never moved by themselves.

categoryAddress.title: A category named like an archived one is made, at the next free address
categoryAddress.text: An archived category keeps its web address for good, but the check before making a category looked only at the categories still shown — so making one again under an archived name failed in the database, with the owner's plan half applied. Now a category still shown with that name is refused as before, and otherwise the new one (or one renamed to that name) takes the next free address. Every way a category is made goes through the same rule.

iphoneInstallSteps.title: The iPhone «install the app» steps follow the Safari in the visitor's hand
iphoneInstallSteps.text: iPhones have no install button, so the site shows steps. On iOS 26 Safari keeps Share inside «⋯» beside the address, so «tap Share» pointed at a button a first-time visitor could not see. The site now reads Safari's own version, the iPad's touch screen and the phone's language. On iOS 26 it shows four steps with Safari's bar drawn, «⋯» ringed and an arrow at that corner, mirrored on an Arabic phone. Older iPhones and the iPad get Share where they keep it. WhatsApp, Facebook and Instagram's built-in browsers, which cannot install at all, are told to open the site in Safari, with a copy-link button. On the Arabic page, Safari's English button names sit isolated beside the Arabic ones, so the right-to-left line stays in order. A check runs sample browser identities through it.

reelsOnPhones.title: The reels on an iPhone, the team's reel editor, and a Facebook share that works from a phone
reelsOnPhones.text: On the owner's iPhone the bottom bar stood in the middle of the screen after watching reels: the player moved between videos with scrollIntoView inside its full-screen layer, which on iOS also shifts the page beneath it. The player now scrolls only itself, and a check refuses that call in any full-screen layer. In the team's reel editor each product is a card with its name and code whole, and the time button says what it sets («show it from 0:12»). Sharing on Facebook from a phone now goes through the phone's share sheet with the link alone (Facebook's web share page opens the app and drops the post), and a kit hands the team the video file and a ready caption, because Facebook plays only videos uploaded to it.

googleReads.title: What Google reads about every page — and a free product feed that never shows a price the shop has not confirmed
googleReads.text: Each page now tells Google what it is, in schema.org data built from the same answers the page shows: the home page the shop itself (its address on the map, opening hours, phones, its pages), a product page the product with its maker's code and a GTIN only when the barcode is the maker's own with a valid check digit, and the price offer only when customers can read that price — most products are still «price on request», so most pages offer none. Product and department pages carry their breadcrumbs, every page its own title (a product's with its maker's code: about 2,400 names are shared) and a canonical address without filters, and search results stay out of the index. A Google Merchant Center feed lists the same products for free, read from the catalogue every 30 minutes. Found live and fixed the same night: a stock call that timed out read as «in stock» — an unread count now never says so.

saleUnit.title: Every product now says the unit it is sold in — and a unit never changes behind a price or a stock count
saleUnit.text: A product carries its sale unit (a piece, a pipe, a metre, a carton, a bag, a kilo, a roll, a set, a can), what one unit holds and in which measure — a 6 m pipe, a carton of 12 pieces, a 25 kg bag. Every product started as one piece holding one piece, so nothing sold changed. The product page says the unit and, where one holds more than one, the price per metre or kilo. A unit changes only on a product that holds no stock and no open document, and on a priced one only when the team confirms the price is the new unit’s; nothing is converted silently, and when the stock service cannot be asked the change is refused rather than guessed. Rehearsed on a copy of the real catalogue before it went live.

listFamilies.title: A supplier’s sizes written three ways still make one product per family — and the maker’s pictures load as you scroll
listFamilies.text: A fittings maker prints an adaptor’s size as «20*25*1/2"», a reducing piece’s as «25*32*20MM» and a valve’s as a bare «75». The size reader now reads all three — a pipe pair before a thread, three diameters, a bare pipe diameter in a list measured in millimetres — so each block of the list becomes one product with its sizes inside: one maker’s 513 codes make 57 products instead of 108. Two products the list names alike are told apart in their names by their sizes’ system, as the maker writes it (metric / BS), and a code made on its own shows its size. The maker’s pictures are fetched as they come into view, four at a time, and the server keeps each for six hours — a phone asking for a hundred at once had shown none. Rehearsed on a copy of the real catalogue before it went live.

reviewOnGoogle.title: Customers are asked for a Google review where it helps — and the printed QR always matches the link
reviewOnGoogle.text: The owner keeps one Google review link in the shop's profile, accepted only as an https link on Google's own hosts. From it the site shows a «review us on Google» button in the footer and on the contact page, a delivered order's page and its delivery mail ask the customer, and the printed invoice carries a small QR of the link in its footer. The panel prints a counter sign in A5 or A4 with a large QR. Every QR is drawn from the saved link, never from an image someone uploaded, and a unit test decodes it back to the link. Nothing shows until the link is set.

wayPricedOnServer.title: The customer picks how the order reaches him — and the server, not the page, decides what that costs
wayPricedOnServer.text: The checkout now offers only the ways the owner opened for that order: collect from the showroom (free, the goods held for his hours, paid there), a driver at his own price, or the shop’s fixed price with its promised days and its discount. The page sends the choice and nothing else; the Orders service asks Shipping what that way costs by the very rule the page showed, before any stock is held — a closed way, a price that changed since it was shown, or no answer refuses the order instead of charging a guess. A made-up fee table that had sat in the code since the start went with it. On the order page the owner sees a pickup’s hold run out, and takes a fixed-price order himself on a day the server keeps within what the customer was promised.

newIndeed.title: Before a price list adds a product, it makes sure the product is new — and a new product’s picture is the maker’s own, found by its own code
newIndeed.text: A supplier’s list no longer creates a product the shop already holds under another code or another name. Each new code is checked against the whole catalogue: the same code with its zeros written otherwise, the shop’s own SKU ending with it, the code written in a product’s name, a model the company’s own products share, or the same name of the same kind and size. A look-alike is shown beside the line with its picture and waits for the owner’s word: «the same» links the line to that product (each size or colour to its own option, never one price for all), «new indeed» lets it be made. For one maker’s fittings, the picture comes from the maker’s own site only where the page states that very code; a family page alone is offered unticked.

moneyIntegrity.title: Four money fixes — a purchase booked receipt by receipt, costs read under the stock lock, a cancellation that holds its invoice, no made-up dashboard figure
moneyIntegrity.text: A purchase received in parts used to be booked whole on its first receipt and never again; now each receipt books its own goods with its share of the freight and the VAT, worked out on what has come so far, so the parts add up to the purchase to the piastre. A purchase works out its new average cost only after the stock row is locked and read again, so a purchase saved a moment before is never averaged away. A cancellation, any status change and a late «payment failed» now hold the invoice’s row: a payment arriving at that moment waits and is refused, and a late failure can no longer cancel an order another payment settled. The statistics drop a «projected revenue» that was the sales × 1.1 and give growth only when there is something to compare with; the dashboard counts the payroll runs still waiting. Each fix came with a test that failed first, was read by a reviewer from five directions, and was rehearsed on copies of the books before going live.

emptyDepartments.title: A department with nothing on show is not shown — and comes back by itself
emptyDepartments.text: Departments whose products were all hidden still appeared in the menu (1,432 ceramics, none published). Now one rule on the server decides: a department is shown to customers only while it is active and a published product sits in it or under it. Every customer read applies it — the menu tree with its sub-levels, the departments page, the home page, the footer, the sitemap and the link preview — and a hidden department’s own address answers like a missing one, with a way back. The team’s panel still lists every department with its shown and total counts. Publishing one product brings the department back within half a minute; the counts are kept briefly so the menu does not count the catalogue on every visit. Here: create an empty department in the panel and it does not appear in the shop.

labelClearestLook.title: Each label picture in its clearest look — the program picks silhouette, lines or tones per product, the team can change it
labelClearestLook.text: After the line drawing went live, the owner asked for whichever look is clearest for each picture. The label code now draws three looks at the thermal printer’s own 8 dots a millimetre — a black silhouette with its inner edges left white, a bold outline with thin inner lines, and three tones in a thin frame — and measures each product at the label’s real size to choose: a thin outline (a chrome tap, a hand shower) reads fastest as a silhouette, a product that fills its whole frame (a water heater) by its lines, a coloured one (a brass cartridge) in tones, a photo taken in a room by its clear edges. Twelve of the shop’s products were printed at true size for the owner before release; the barcode-printing screen lets the team override the look per product, remembered per photo. The labels check tests the chooser’s rules one by one and each look on photos it makes itself, besides reading every barcode back.

deliveryWays.title: Three ways to receive an order, each the owner’s to open — and a label that shows the product to someone who cannot read
deliveryWays.text: Customers will choose between collecting from the showroom (free, held for the hours the owner sets, paid there), a driver at his own price for the governorate (the system that already ran, untouched), or the shop’s own fixed price per governorate — light parcel or heavy, promised in so many days, free from an amount worked out from the share of an order the owner agrees to pay for delivery, with stepped discounts on the way. Each way is his switch; until he opens one, the checkout runs exactly as before, which the tests hold. On the warehouse side, every printed barcode label can now carry the product’s picture beside its name: the product’s outline in black with its body in light dots, made at the label printer’s own 8 dots a millimetre, so a worker who does not read knows the box at a glance — and the labels check still reads every barcode back.

searchOpen.title: The shop opened to search engines — and the list of its pages is the catalogue itself, never a file that grows old
searchOpen.text: While the shop was a closed trial, robots.txt kept every search engine out and the sitemap was a placeholder: seven pages and the words «SITE_ORIGIN» where the address belonged. The owner opened the site to everyone, then asked for it to be found. Now search engines may read the shop — never the team's panel, a customer's own pages or the sign-in — and /sitemap.xml is written by the catalogue service each time it is asked: the shop's pages, every department and every product a customer can see, at the real address, with the day each product last changed. A product hidden is out of it at once; 16,668 addresses on the first day. Beside «install the app» the menus now offer «add us as a preferred source on Google».

sharedLink.title: A product sent on WhatsApp arrives as the product — its picture, name and code — and the message says who writes and why
sharedLink.text: A link to a product used to arrive in a chat as the shop's logo and name, whatever was sent. Chat apps read a link before anybody opens it, and a single-page shop has nothing to show them until its scripts run. Now the server writes a small preview for the robots of WhatsApp, Facebook, Telegram and the rest — the product's own first picture, its name, brand, department and code, and its price only when customers may read it — and the front sends only those robots, and only on a product's or a department's address, to it; a person always gets the page. A hidden product, or the home page, still reads as the shop with its logo. The WhatsApp buttons changed with it: every one of them, from the bottom bar to the footer, now opens with who is writing — the name and mobile number from the account, or typed once — with no greeting, then why (a product, a price statement, an order, a design) and the page's details with its link. One hook makes all of them, and the UI audit refuses a WhatsApp link written any other way.

fittingsTree.title: Pipe fittings sorted the way a plumber asks for them: the kind first, then the material
fittingsTree.text: Six hundred pipe fittings sat in a few crowded departments, supply and drain mixed, an elbow beside a tee beside a cap. The owner asked for a tree a customer can walk: elbows apart, tees apart, unions apart, caps apart, and the supply fittings never confused with the drain ones. Supply fittings now open by kind, and each kind by its material — PPR, pressure UPVC, pressure polypropylene, galvanised iron; drain fittings by kind; every name says «supply» or «drain». The plan went to the owner product by product before anything moved; one transaction then made 32 departments, renamed 22 and placed 585 products, with its own checks inside (no product on a parent, a picture for every department, three names each) and an undo rehearsed on a copy first.

ownCodeFirst.title: A code typed brings the product it belongs to first — before one that only carries it on an option
ownCodeFirst.text: The search watch, which tries the real search every six hours, caught a jacuzzi's own code bringing a same-named twin first: the twin's colour option carried the same maker's code, both stood on the line «found by its code», and the tie-breaks chose the twin. The code line now has two steps — first the product's own codes (its SKU, model, maker's code, its own barcode), then the codes it answers to through another record (an option's code or barcode, a SKU it carried before); the start of a code the same way. The twin is still found, and still before everything found by its words. Measured read-only on the live catalogue: of 57 searches, only the jacuzzi codes changed, each now opening with its own product, in the same time. The watch now types every such code each round. A review board read it, and each step of the rule has a test on a real database that fails without it.

oneFamily.title: A maker's fitting in sixteen sizes becomes one product with its sizes inside — not sixteen products of one name
oneFamily.text: A pipe-fittings maker prints one table per fitting: an elbow in sixteen diameters, a saddle in eighteen pipe-and-thread sizes, each size its own article code. Made one code at a time, that list would have been five hundred products, many with the same name. Now the codes of one table — the same name, the code printed over the table, every size read by the shop's own size reader — become one product, each size an option carrying the maker's code, so the next list prices each size where it belongs. A size the shop's sizes table lacks is added through the table's own door, and the card says which before anything is made. The size reader learned two things on the way: «1 1/4"» is one size, and «20*1/2"» is a 20 mm pipe with a half-inch thread, never twenty inches. On a copy of the live catalogue the list's 513 codes became 108 products, none refused. A review board read it before it went live.

listsAsPrinted.title: Two more makers' price lists read as printed — their colours, their series, their Arabic letters, a fittings maker's families — and nothing read before goes uncounted
listsAsPrinted.text: A sanitaryware maker's luxury list prints colours the reader did not know (calacatta, platinum, special colours, wood), writes each series name turned up the side of its table, and sets some Arabic letters as one shape or inside the letter before them. A pipe-fittings maker prints no name column at all: each table is named by the family printed over it, with its sizes in a column of their own. The reader now reads the colours (a wood beside a material is no colour), the turned series as the section of its table's lines, the Arabic letters in their order and an Arabic line right to left with its numbers and English kept in theirs, and each fitting by its family with its size apart, so a family can become one product with its sizes as options. A review board of three read it and set ten musts; each was answered with a test that fails without its fix. Every list the shop has uploaded was read again: the spreadsheets read exactly as before, and every price read before is read or counted now.

sameThing.title: A maker's price reaches a product only when it is the same thing — and never by itself when it is twice the shop's price or half
sameThing.text: A check of the live catalogue against the newest list found lines priced on the wrong thing: a whole toilet or a bathroom set reached by the line of the bowl alone, a bowl carrying the code of its tank, a set of three mixers reached by one mixer. Now the program reads what a line and a product are — a bowl, a toilet, a close-coupled toilet, a tank, a seat, a basin, a pedestal, a shower tray, a bath, a mixer, a set — from the words the maker's list and the shop's own names both use. A line of another thing is held back from the prices, with the reason beside it, until a person chooses the product by hand; a new price twice the shop's or half of it waits for a person's tick, line by line. A thing not named is never called different: on a copy of the live catalogue the guard held exactly the fifteen wrong lines and no right one. A review board read it, and it was walked on a phone and a desktop, before it went live.

makersOwnList.title: A maker's own price list read as its page shows it — and nothing it holds vanishes
makersOwnList.text: A maker's list prints an item's name over several lines with its code and price on the last, its column titles over several rows, its sizes in front of its codes and its notes across the page. The reader now finds the page's own two spacings — the lines of one item and the gap between items — and gives each priced line the name lines of its own block, above it or around it; a name over several variants names each of them. One maker's 88-page list went from 139 lines read to 605, covering 430 of its 443 article numbers, with no AI. On the way, an older class was closed: a second code beside the first, a price that had run into a name, and a price under a colour the reader does not know are now counted and left for a person, never passed by. On the eleven real lists read again, no code's price changed. A review board read it twice — prices pass every gate — and every rule has a test that fails without it.

newFromList.title: A maker's new products from its own price list — with the maker's own picture, or none
newFromList.text: A maker's list arrives with products the shop has never carried. One card on the list's review now groups those codes by kind, each group in the category where the maker's own products of that kind already sit (offered as sure only when most of them, and at least three, do); the owner confirms a group with one press. The products are made hidden and with no price, through the same door as every product (code, barcode, names in each language), and the list then prices them when it is applied. A code already in the catalogue — even filed under a shorter model code, archived, or another maker's — is never made twice. Each product's picture comes only from the maker's own website, and only when the site's model, kind and placement (wall-hung, floor, above counter…) all match the line; otherwise there is no picture rather than a guessed one. Products changed since are never taken back. A review board read it before it went live.

groupKinds.title: Discounts by kind of goods, with exceptions: the nearest rule wins
groupKinds.text: A maker discounts its mixers, baths, ceramics, shower enclosures and spare parts differently. A company's discount groups can now be made from the shop's own categories (mixers = the mixers category and everything under it), beside the groups by series, and a single product can carry a discount of its own. A product takes the nearest discount: the product alone, then its model, then its kind, then its category, then the company's one discount — and one category never carries two discounts (the screen refuses the second and says which group prices it). One press can give every group the same discount, but a group with a discount of its own is changed only when ticked. One maker's 1,855 products fell into nine groups with none left over; made with no discount of their own, they moved no price — a whole re-pricing on a copy of the catalogue ticked nothing. A review board read it before it went live.

companyGroups.title: One maker, several discounts: a company's product groups priced apart
companyGroups.text: A maker sells its economy line at a final price and its other lines at a list discount — so the shop buys and sells them at different discounts. A company now has groups, each named by its series (Duravit's own Egyptian list gives three: economy at a final price, local, imported), and each group carries the owner's two ways of pricing: his discount from the company and the customer's, or net plus his profit. A product finds its group by a series name in its own name, Arabic or English, as whole words; before a discount is set the owner sees exactly which products a group takes, and can take one out by hand (an acrylic bath that shares a ceramic set's series name). A group's rule comes before its category's; everything else is priced as before, and nothing changes a price until a review is applied. A review board read it twice — money changes pass every gate — and it was rehearsed on a copy of the catalogue: an economy basin priced at net + 15 %, a local toilet at 30 % / 25 %, the economy group priced again alone.

pdfArabicFonts.title: A supplier PDF whose Arabic font hides its letters, read right
pdfArabicFonts.text: One maker's price list draws Arabic letters under Latin codes («%» for «ح», «T» for «ف») and some digits as accents, so «لحوض» came out as «ل%وض» and «58» as «٥̕». The reader now gives each font's codes back — per font, because two weights of the same font code them differently — and only what the file's own words prove: a code is mapped when the words it sits in become real words of the catalogue, a digit when the English beside it says which. Damaged names on that list fell from 225 to 7; no code, colour or price changed on any of the eleven real lists read again.

colourOptions.title: A supplier prices a basin in white and in pergamon — the shop now sells it in both
colourOptions.text: A maker's list prices one code in each colour, while the catalogue held the product without colours: both prices fell on one product, and someone had to drop one, line by line — 797 lines on the Ideal Standard list. One card on the review now gives each such product its colours from the colours table, each its own price, its own code and its own barcode; the first colour keeps the product's barcode, so labels already printed still scan. It touches only products nothing holds: before any change the catalogue asks the warehouse (stock, reservations, purchases, transfers, counts) and the invoices (quotes, drafts, open invoices, returns), and when either cannot answer it does nothing. The owner sees first what it will do; what he saw is what is done; taking it back leaves any product priced or held since. The team previews, the owner presses. A review board held the first version over stock it would have moved; the second moves none, was read twice, and was rehearsed on copies of three services' books: 797 lines down to 208, the rest left on purpose with their reasons.

priceListScreens.title: The price lists, from upload to undo, as a shop owner reads them — and a line read whole
priceListScreens.text: The owner asked for the whole way of a supplier's list to be easy, and approved the design before it was built. Upload is one button, in the order he reads: the file, the company, the date written on the list (never today by itself), the selling price in one sentence, then «upload and read». While a 79-page PDF is read the screen says which page. The review opens on three tiles and one next step; a phone gets a card per line with buttons a finger hits; every question is the shop's own window, its answer in words. A list can be read again from its kept file — a price the owner typed or a product he chose by hand stays on its line. The reader learned to keep the words between an English and an Arabic name column (a grey and a walnut unit no longer read as one), to give back the joined Arabic letters a font leaves unreadable, and never to put a line, by its name, on a product that carries another maker's code — it names the model's relative instead. Two independent reviews read the change; each finding became a test.

priceLookup.title: One search box over every supplier list, and a link the customer can open
priceLookup.text: The team searches every price list the owner uploaded — by code, name or colour — and sees the company's price, the shop's selling price, the change from the list before, and a product's price through the years. For customers there is one link, off until the owner switches it on: every applied list by its date, newest first, as a plain table and a PDF with the shop's identity — the shop's confirmed selling prices only, never the company's. The owner can hide any list; a hidden one is refused by the server, not only hidden on the page.

pdfPriceLists.title: Supplier price lists in PDF, read here from their own words — and checked by nine reviews
pdfPriceLists.text: The owner could not upload his 79-page Ideal Standard list: a PDF was read only by an AI service, out of credit, and a file that size filled the server’s memory. The shop now reads a PDF itself: each page’s words and where they stand become a table — its columns from the strips most lines leave empty, one set for the whole page, cut where a table of its own leaves a gap; prices per colour, stacked and side-by-side tables, Arabic tables laid out right to left, a header on two rows, a band of price words over a lower table. The rule is the owner’s: a price never goes to the wrong code, colour or item, and no line vanishes — a line the reader is not sure of is left, counted, with its reason. Nine independent reviews attacked it with constructed layouts; each finding became a test (about 300 now), and a rehearsal on his 11 real lists reads the same after every round — Ideal Standard 974 → 1,270 lines. No line read from a PDF, or from a sheet holding more than one table, ticks itself: the owner sees each beside the original page before any price changes.

ownerSwitches.title: Every on / off switch of the shop on one page — the owner’s alone
ownerSwitches.text: The owner asked to decide himself what shows, what works and what is switched off. One page now gathers the shop’s 21 switches in six groups, each with what it does and its state read from its own service; a read that fails shows «—», never a guess. A simple switch is pressed right there, through the same door its own page uses, so the server’s checks stay in one place; the others open the page that holds them. Three that lived in server settings or in the code became buttons: the customers’ order e-mails (asked twice — they reach people outside the shop), the lock on product codes, and search by photo. Each is one row with who pressed it and when, read at every use so a press works at once; with no row the shop behaves exactly as before. The codes lock replaced two constants: every writer of a code (the re-code, a move, a category’s or brand’s new code, a product’s edit, the duplicate merges) asks the one switch, and the first close is kept as the day the project really started, so replaced codes stay findable for good even if he opens the codes again. Tests press each switch both ways, and a planted fault (the switch ignored) makes them fail.

phoneSideways.title: A phone on its side, and an installed app that never jumps when it is turned
phoneSideways.text: From the owner’s photos of his iPhone turned sideways: the bars stay one slim line, the page uses the whole width, the colours reach the screen’s edges while the words keep clear of the notch, and the panel’s sheets open as a card in the middle. The app on the home screen used to start below the phone’s clock; turned and back, iOS kept the old height — a purple band at the top and the bottom bar floating up by the clock’s height. It now covers the whole screen and keeps clear of the clock itself (a translucent status bar and the safe-area insets in CSS). Static audits guard each piece, and each catches a planted fault.

evidenceLedger.title: Every requirement in one register, and a ledger that says «verified» only for a check that ran
evidenceLedger.text: Months of the owner’s directives were consolidated into one register of requirements — with the contradictions between them and his decision on each — a phased roadmap, and a verification ledger. A row reads VERIFIED only when its check was executed (or reuses a recorded run), otherwise FAILED or NEEDS VERIFICATION. The baseline was taken on a clean copy: the full build, every unit test, the front-end audits and the integration suite on PostgreSQL. It surfaced two guards that had gone unchecked while CI was paused; both were fixed and green again the same night.

feedbackQueue.title: One queue for every problem and idea — what people report and what the program catches by itself
feedbackQueue.text: The site says it is being tried and asks for help: a slim bar on every shop page, a link in the footer and a bug button in the team’s panel open one sheet — a problem, an idea or a note, in the person’s own words, with one screenshot from the camera or the gallery; the page, the kind of device and the site’s version go with it by themselves, and nothing else. A visitor may leave a mobile or an email; a signed-in person reads the shop’s answer under «My reports». The pages also report by themselves, quietly and once a visit: a screen that crashed (the crash screen says the shop already knows and asks what the person was doing) and any call the server failed. The same fault is one line that counts how often it happened — its fingerprint ignores the build’s file names, line numbers and ids — and a fault marked fixed that happens again opens again by itself. The owner works one queue with what waits first, a note for the team and an answer for the person; screenshots stay private and are erased sixty days after an item is closed. The same day the shop’s own words put its standing and its technical know-how first, with the year it began said only once the owner writes it.

attendanceDevices.title: The owner picks each attendance device by a six-digit code — and the attendance pages show only the way he chose
attendanceDevices.text: Any phone can become an attendance device without anyone signing in on it: it opens the attendance screen, keeps a key of its own and shows a six-digit code for ten minutes; the owner types that code and a name («the shop’s phone», «my phone») on his settings page, and within seconds the device shows the workers’ names. Each device is renamed or removed in one tap, and every record carries the name of the device it was taken on. The owner also chooses how his workers record — on these devices with a picture, by scanning the code on the wall with their own phones, or both — and what he did not choose disappears everywhere and is refused by the server: no scan button, no distance figures, no device tiles that would only fail. The door camera stays out of sight until it is set up, a leave is written in one place only, and the menu keeps each worker’s own page apart from the owner’s attendance management.

menuSections.title: Attendance and hiring, each a section of its own in the panel
menuSections.text: At the owner’s word, attendance and hiring left the staff group. «My attendance» — every worker’s own page — stands alone in the menu; «Attendance management» holds the owner’s seven pages — today, the month, working hours, leave, the leave calendar, the review and the settings — each at its own address; «Hiring» holds the job ads and the applications. Each person sees only what he may open, and the page on screen is lit in the menu. A link lives once: the menu is the one way between the pages, and no page repeats its section’s links on top (the panel’s check refuses one that does).

attendancePhone.title: An old phone at the door becomes the shop’s attendance device — tap your name, smile, done
attendancePhone.text: The owner’s idea: instead of a tablet or face-recognition hardware, a phone that never leaves the shop. Every worker’s name stands in a big tile, green for coming in, orange for going out; a tap opens the front camera, counts 3-2-1 and takes his picture, and the screen fills green or orange with his name, the time and a sound of its own. Nobody is signed in on it: the owner, signed in once, gives the phone its own key — kept on the phone, only a fingerprint of it on the server — and his session leaves the phone; its three doors take only that key and stay open while the shop is closed to visitors. When the line drops, taps are kept on the phone and sent at their own time when it returns, marked «sent late» for the owner. No face is recognised: the picture sits beside the mark for the owner, erased after 30 days, and setting the phone up makes every worker read the privacy notice again.

doorCamera.title: The door camera’s picture of each attendance scan — no tablet, no face recognition
doorCamera.text: Instead of a tablet at the door, the owner chose the camera he already has: an EZVIZ camera on the shop’s own Wi-Fi, with no recorder. The moment a worker scans the code, a picture of that moment from the door camera is kept beside his mark, so the owner sees who actually stood there — a photo of the code sent home, or a colleague scanning for a friend, shows. The worker is answered at once; the picture follows a moment later through a small local helper that reads one frame of the camera’s stream. The camera is reached on the shop’s private network — or, when the server stands elsewhere, through EZVIZ’s own cloud with the owner’s developer keys, the way its app reaches the camera — its code is never shown again or logged, the pictures are the owner’s alone and are erased after 30 days, and switching the camera on makes every worker read the privacy notice again.

attendanceTwo.title: Attendance, second phase — right numbers, nobody in his own record, and Egypt’s year on one calendar
attendanceTwo.text: A committee of four departments (security, payroll, labour and data law, the shop floor) studied the first phase; the owner said «go on». Days before attendance began read «not followed», never absent; Egypt’s official holidays (the labour minister’s twelve occasions, fifteen paid days) are put in each year by themselves — the Hijri feasts «expected» until announced — and the Christians’ own feasts show for everyone and are a day off for the people the owner ticks, with no religion stored; a leave over a holiday or a day off does not count it. Hours carry the day they began, so a change never rewrites the past, and a season such as Ramadan has its own hours. Nobody but the owner writes in his own record; what a manager writes or cancels waits for the owner’s review, at most seven days back, beside a daily list of what may need a look (no place, far, weak signal, a new phone, a phone two people scanned from). The scan from the camera now waits for one tap and answers full-screen in green or orange with its own sound; the same scan again says «already recorded». Before his first scan a worker reads — or hears — what is kept and why (Egypt’s data law), and the phone’s exact place is erased after 90 days. Casual leave follows the new law (seven days within the annual ones), with maternity, paternity, Hajj and exams; every worker sees the whole year on a calendar.

attendance.title: Attendance by the shop’s QR code, and leave — shown first, never charged
attendance.text: Each employee scans the code on the shop’s wall with his phone — with the page’s button, or with the phone’s own camera, since the code is the page’s address. A day’s scans alternate in, out, in again (he may step out and come back); the phone’s place is compared with the shop’s and a far scan is shown, never refused. The owner’s board reads each day: present, still in, absent, on leave, late and early against that person’s own hours, the times he stepped out; a forgotten scan is written with its reason, a wrong one cancelled, never deleted. Leave is asked, answered and counted against the Labour Law of 2025 (15 / 21 / 30 days). The first phase only shows — nothing touches a salary until the owner asks — and the board and leave answers are his until he grants them. The same evening the date boxes kept to their column on every screen, the balances followed an answer without reopening the page, a scan opened by the phone’s camera while signed out was kept through the sign-in, and a committee of four departments — security, payroll, labour and data law, the shop floor — wrote what comes next: right numbers (holidays, dated hours, a «tracked from» day), cheap locks against abuse (nobody touches his own record, the owner reviews hand-written marks), a one-tap confirm, and the law’s steps before any deduction.

outagePage.title: Something shows in every outage — even when the shop’s computer is off
outagePage.text: A paused site already showed the shop’s «back shortly» page, and an open page a strip when the server went silent. Now, when the computer, its tunnel or Docker is down and nothing of the shop can answer, a small Cloudflare Worker in front of the domain answers a page visit with that same page — built from it, the logo inside, never cached — while a call of the program gets the error as it is. A build check fails if the page changes and the Worker does not; a check runs it against a site that answers, one Cloudflare cannot reach and one that is gone. Tried live: the tunnel off for 16 seconds, the shop’s page shown. The page then got a language choice at its top — Arabic, English and German in production, English and German here — kept across its own refresh.

shopIdentity.title: Who the shop is became a setting — the first step to serving another shop
shopIdentity.text: The shop’s names in three languages, its logo, phones, email, address, map, opening hours, tax number and commercial register now live on one settings page the owner edits; the header, the footer, the contact page, the call buttons and the sign-in pages read them from there, and a field left empty falls back to the value the code held, so nothing he has not touched changes. The server refuses a wrong phone, a map that is not Google’s, a tax number that is not nine digits, or a logo the program does not keep itself. Since the same day the PDFs print the uploaded logo, the names, phones, tax number and commercial register from it (the services fetch the logo only when it changes, and draw it only if it is a PNG, JPEG or WebP under 2 MB), the customers’ mails and the reset-code text name the shop from it, and so do the legal pages and the pages printed from the browser. Then the paused-site page (which may call nothing) began reading a copy of these details the site leaves on the visitor’s device, mails went out under the shop’s name, and the owner’s alerts to its email. What is fixed at build time — the app manifest, the currency, time zone and phone rules — waits for a second shop, the way to running the same program for another one.

understoodSearch.title: The search knows what it asks for — the thing itself first
understoodSearch.text: Every product is read as a merchant reads it: by the thing its name begins with (⁨«حوض مطبخ»⁩ is a sink; ⁨«مصفاة حوض مطبخ»⁩ a strainer, though it holds both words). A search is read the same way in Arabic, English and German, and the products that ARE the thing asked for come first. In production: about 150 kinds across every department, each product’s reading kept and read again by itself when the product or the knowledge changes — ⁨«Toilette»⁩ now opens with toilets, not a paper holder.

threeLanguages.title: One search in Arabic, English and German
threeLanguages.text: The same rules in every language: Arabic is found after its article, a German part inside the word it builds (⁨«Armatur»⁩ in ⁨«Waschtischarmatur»⁩), an English word only whole (⁨«bath»⁩ never inside ⁨«bathroom»⁩). In production the German names joined the search text gradually, the search answering all along.

amazonOrder.title: Like Amazon: the product asked for first
amazonOrder.text: Among products found equally well: the owner’s pick, then a product before its spare part, the category most results are of, a listing with a photo and a price, the most viewed — and the same name never twice in a row. A name that says the opposite of a word typed comes after.

searchWatch.title: The search is watched on the real catalogue
searchWatch.text: After every deploy and every six hours the program searches its own shop as a customer: the trade’s words with the fewest and the most results they may bring, every search a customer made that found products, the sorted list and the categories against the search, codes and hidden products. A failure is on the owner’s screen at once, and a deploy waits for the first round.

listKit.title: One way every list searches, pages and dates
listKit.text: Every list — on the server and on the screens — now searches, pages and filters by date one way: every word in any order, a code without its dashes, a whole Cairo day, the newest question wins. Tests fail the build when a new screen writes its own.

marketWords.title: Search reads the trade's own words
marketWords.text: ⁨«كرسي»⁩ finds toilets, ⁨«نيبل»⁩ finds what is written ⁨«نبل»⁩, ⁨«بي بي ار»⁩ finds PPR and ⁨«اطقم»⁩ finds sets. In production too: a word typed alone is looked for even when it usually only describes, a sorted search counts everything it found, and a correction shoppers accepted waits for the owner before it changes what any word means.

categoryFilters.title: Category filters that keep their word
categoryFilters.text: Filters live in the page's address, so «back» from a product keeps them and another category starts clean. Every maker, size and finish of the whole category is counted on the server, and a filter is offered only when its data is real.

wordStart.title: A short word finds the words it begins
wordStart.text: Typing ⁨«بان»⁩ now finds ⁨بانيو⁩ and ⁨«حو»⁩ finds ⁨حوض⁩, while a short word never matches inside another word.

supplierCheques.title: Cheques to suppliers, and suppliers' opening balances
supplierCheques.text: A cheque carries its number and due date and is cashed once; a cheque cancelled at the moment it is cashed is never both. Opening balances of suppliers, and each supplier entered once.

categoryPictures.title: Every category has a picture
categoryPictures.text: Thirty-one empty categories took a picture of their own type, each one checked by eye; the web is now one of the sources.

productReading.title: The program reads a product like a merchant
productReading.text: It reads a product's name as kind, material, colour and joint, proposes its category, and learns from what the owner teaches it. Nothing moves without his say.

reviews.title: Reviews wait for the shop
reviews.text: A review is published only after the shop reads it, and waits again when its writer changes it; «verified purchase» is read from the orders' books.

siteNumbers.title: The site counts its own visits
siteNumbers.text: Visits and purchases counted by the shop itself, with no cookie and nothing kept about the person; the owner decides what customers see.

jobs.title: Jobs: the owner posts an ad, people apply, the team calls them
jobs.text: The owner writes a job ad in Arabic and the program words its English and German; a «Jobs» page anyone applies from in a minute — even while the shop is closed — with a name, an Egyptian mobile and a governorate, and an applications screen with a badge for the new ones and a call or WhatsApp in one tap. Photos of a CV stay closed until the owner turns them on with one switch; then they are cleaned of camera data by the same code that cleans customers’ photos.

everyLevelSearch.title: Search at every level: whatever a worker knows of a thing finds it
everyLevelSearch.text: An invoice by its number typed without dashes, by the customer’s phone typed any way (010… or +20…), or by a product on it under today’s name in any language or its code — though the line keeps the name it was sold under. In production: invoices, price statement requests, returns, purchases, transfers, deliveries, the day-book, receivables and payables, and Ctrl K searches every list at once. Try it here on the back office’s orders.

hiddenOptions.title: A hidden option is the team’s — a shopper never finds the product by it
hiddenOptions.text: A colour or size the team hid on a product was still in its search text: a shopper found the product by its colour, code or barcode. Now every product has two texts: the shown one everybody searches, the hidden one only the team — proved on a real PostgreSQL.

marketingMenu.title: Ads, coupons and points are a menu group of their own
marketingMenu.text: On the owner’s word, the marketing screens left «Sales» for a «Marketing» group — and the menu is still guarded by a check that refuses a group of more than nine links or a link without its name in three languages.

categoryPricing.title: Each company priced category by category — the owner’s two ways, its cost kept
categoryPricing.text: The owner picks a company and sees only its categories, as a tree; he ticks some and gives them a way: «a discount on the list» (cost = the list less his discount, sale = the list less the customer’s) or «net + profit». A category without one takes the one above it, then the company’s. The list price is kept on every product and colour, so a changed rule is priced again, reviewed before it applies and undone at will; the company’s sheet goes out as Excel and comes back edited; the purchase invoice proposes the cost from the list. The cost is seen only by who may change prices or buy — rehearsed on a copy of the real catalogue: a first re-pricing changed 0 of 3,921 prices. A list may hold the 14 % VAT or not: each company has a switch and each list may say otherwise, and a purchase tax invoice is proposed the cost without the VAT, since it adds it below.

priceListsPlain.title: The price-lists committee: each list says what it waits for
priceListsPlain.text: The owner found the price lists hard, so a committee of the people who use them (purchasing, pricing, catalogue, accounts, sales, testing) read them end to end: each list now says its next step in words with «needs your decision» first, its lines in three plain groups (sure / to look at / no product found), an unsure line shows the product’s photo with «right / wrong» in one tap, a re-pricing that changes nothing makes no list, and «the lists still missing» per company.

shopDays.title: The day is the shop’s — Cairo’s, not Greenwich’s
shopDays.text: The books, the stock and the money totals cut the day at UTC midnight (02:00 or 03:00 in the shop): a sale at 00:30 landed on the day before, «to day X» lost the whole last day, and a stock card asked from a day began at zero. Now the day page, trial balance, income statement, balance sheet, debt ages, reports and revenue read Cairo’s day, the stock card opens with its opening balance, a coupon runs whole days and every document number takes the shop’s year. Done through the six gates: tests that failed on the old code, a five-direction review, a rehearsal on a copy of the data.

reportsFromBooks.title: The dashboard and the reports read the books
reportsFromBooks.text: The dashboard read a separate tally nothing filled, so it showed zero while the books held the month’s invoices. Now the month’s revenue, the invoice count and average, and the sales, purchases and cash-flow reports are read from the books by the shop’s day: invoices after discounts, returns and cancellations, before VAT — the income statement’s figure to the piastre — and purchases on the day they were received. The owner was asked first; a test failed on the old code; a five-direction review; a rehearsal on a copy of the data.

phoneMenu.title: The phone menu fits one screen
phoneMenu.text: It was eleven rows one under the other. Now: a greeting with your name, the team’s panel as one button, your account’s pages as tiles three a row (orders, price statements, favourites with their count, points, e-mail settings), then «Shop» with four links. It opens right under the bar instead of under the language button. The owner saw it in two screenshots before it went live.

marketFold.title: The dollar and gold watch folds and opens
marketFold.text: On the dashboard, the market card (dollar, euro, copper, gold) now has an arrow beside its title: folded it is one line with the title and the last update, and it opens back as it was. Each device remembers the choice. On the price-freshness page it stays open, since there it is the subject. And the big title card at the top of the dashboard is gone, at the owner’s word: the bar and the side menu already name the page, so it now opens on the shortcuts. The «back to the shop» button beside the search went too: the shop’s own bar always sits above the panel. The figures under it («The shop’s figures») fold the same way, to one line: the month’s revenue and its invoices — one arrow for every group: «Latest orders» and «Best sellers» fold the same way. And first on the dashboard now, always in sight: «Stock and money alerts» — what the shop stocks that ran out or is about to, and what customers owe and suppliers are owed (the same totals as their pages).

panelStrip.title: The panel’s menu became a strip of icons
panelStrip.text: On a laptop the long menu (14 groups and a block of pinned tiles) is now a narrow strip: «Pinned», then each group as its icon over its name. A press opens the group’s pages beside the strip, over the page; choosing a page, Escape or a press outside closes it, and the page keeps the width the old menu took. Groups went from 14 to 11; barcode printing stays one press. A phone keeps its drawer. The owner saw three ways, asked to see this one on the real screen, then approved it. The design audit now refuses a bottom bar that writes the side’s width as a number of its own. And on the phone: ☰ opens the eleven sections as tiles, three a row, on one screen; a section shows its pages with «All sections» to go back, and the pinned pages stay in the bottom bar. And the phone’s bottom bar of shortcuts now fits the screen: the person’s first four and «More», never sliding sideways; «Edit the bar» orders them with arrows, takes them off and adds any page he may open. What each person sets up for himself — his shortcuts and their order, the folded groups, his recent pages, his language — is now kept with his account and follows him to every phone and laptop he signs in on; only a device’s own things (the phone’s voice, a count kept offline) stay on the device, and a design check refuses any other way.

stockCounts.title: Stock counts in sessions: workers count blind, only the owner writes
stockCounts.text: A supervisor opens a count on a warehouse's shelves. A worker counts on his phone by pictures: the shelf's big number in its room's colour, scan the shelf label (a wrong shelf turns red with a buzz), every scanned piece shows the product's photo and a big number, with − / + and a digits-only pad. He never sees the books (a blind count). Finishing a shelf writes the books' quantity beside each line; what the books hold but nobody found counts as zero. «Count differences» are priced at today's cost, and «Approve» is the owner's alone: written shelf by shelf, each shelf whole or not at all, and sales made after the count are not counted twice. An independent review found 2 blockers and 7 fixes — all fixed — and a rehearsal on a database copy found two more (one in the stock door itself), fixed with tests. Then, from the owner trying it: a shelf taken by mistake can be let go (it waits again for its label, nothing in stock moves); a 🔊 beside every sentence and name reads it aloud with the phone’s best voice (an Egyptian one first, and a «Choose the voice» sheet to try the others), the spoken sentences written with their vowels; and a barcode nobody knows is looked up by name or number. And, at the owner’s word on the cost of a first count («keep it zero, with the possibility to edit it»): a product counted for the first time in a warehouse is worth 0 until the owner types its cost per piece before «Approve» — written as its opening balance (the owner’s equity), also for pieces sold before it was ever counted. The independent review found that case (a blocker) and two smaller ones; all fixed, with tests that failed first, and tried on a database copy. Counting is now a section of its own in the panel’s menu. From the owner trying it again: the voice names the warehouse and the place together («Al-Malak warehouse, place 1, the entrance»), in the voice chosen in the phone’s own settings; and a product’s code typed in any scan box (its SKU or the maker’s code, dashes and case ignored) finds it like its barcode — a design check now refuses a scan box that would drop a typed code. A word the phone’s voice reads wrong — «warehouse» (makhzan) — is now given its vowels before it is said. The owner can now teach the voice himself: a page lists a word as it is written and how it is said, with a button to hear it, and every phone of the shop says it his way at once. The counting screen then took the panel’s own sizes (the owner found it bigger than the rest): its photos, room colours, numbers and voice carry it, not size — and a design check refuses anything bigger anywhere in the panel.

priceGate.title: A price from a supplier’s list reaches the shop only as the owner saw it
priceGate.text: Reading a price list is now checked end to end. Every line of a file is counted — read, or left with its reason (on request, a number that reads two ways, a total line, another currency); hidden sheets, rows and columns are never read, a table beside a table is read too, and the column each price came from is named. A number is read one way or not at all: «1.250» is 1,250 only where its column has no decimals, «350 400» is two prices, not 350,400. Nothing risky ticks itself — a first price, a product «on request», a change of 25 % or more, an unsure match, a market-price list. Before anything changes, the apply window shows what the server works out on the live prices: every risky line one by one (with a price typed over the file’s shown beside it), and the lines it holds back, which one tap unticks; it applies exactly what was shown, or nothing. Only the owner approves; undoing a list never takes back a price a newer list set, and a list that ever priced something is kept as its history.

taxInvoiceOnRequest.title: An online order is a regular invoice — the customer asks for a tax invoice, and the shop issues it from the Tax Authority
taxInvoiceOnRequest.text: In Egypt the official tax invoice comes out of the Tax Authority’s e-invoice system, so a website order is now a regular invoice with no VAT. At checkout the customer may tick «I need a tax invoice» for a company (its name and tax number) or a person (a name and the national ID); the 14 % VAT is added and shown in the total before he confirms, and the page says the shop issues the invoice and gets in touch. The team finds those orders under one filter, sees for whom on the order, and marks the tax invoice sent with its number in the authority’s system once the order is paid; the customer’s «My orders» says it was asked for, then sent. A switch for «tax invoices issued directly» stays locked until the direct link with the Tax Authority works.

etaLinkScreen.title: The link with the Tax Authority is kept from a screen — its secret sealed, and nothing unsigned is ever sent
etaLinkScreen.text: The owner now keeps the shop’s link with Egypt’s e-invoice system on one screen: the trial or the real system, the login details the authority gave the shop, and the shop as the authority knows it. The client secret is write-only — sealed with AES-GCM under a key derived from the services’ own secret, never shown back, never in a log or the audit; an empty field keeps it. «Test the connection» logs in at the system’s fixed address and remembers the answer. The orders service reads the link through an internal door every five minutes and lays it over its own settings without a restart. The screen lists every step, the real system and the e-signature last: on the trial system, or until the signer with the owner’s USB token exists, the link never counts as working and no document is sent, because the authority refuses an unsigned invoice.

payTheShop.title: The shop’s own InstaPay link, address and wallet — written by the owner, shown to a customer whose order waits for payment
payTheShop.text: In «Shop details» the owner writes where customers can pay the shop by themselves: an InstaPay payment link (only InstaPay’s own https addresses are kept), an InstaPay address (name@instapay) and a mobile wallet number (an Egyptian mobile). A customer whose order waits for its payment sees them after ordering and in «My orders»: one tap opens InstaPay, one tap copies the address or the number. The team confirms the payment when it arrives, as before; a card gateway comes next, on the same screen.

filesSection.title: One menu section for files, prices and automation
filesSection.text: Everything that turns a file into data — price lists, products from photos, the data review queue, the product understanding, the learned rules and the automation jobs — now sits in one section of the admin menu, «Files & automation», instead of being spread over three. The menu’s own audit keeps every section at eight links at most, each with its page and its three names.

cardGateway.title: A card gateway behind one seam — keys sealed, every result signed, checked, kept and acted on once
cardGateway.text: Card payment goes through one interface for any payment company, with Paymob (Egypt) as the first adapter. The owner keeps the gateway on one screen: the secret key and the HMAC secret are write-only and sealed with AES-GCM, and a key of the other system (trial / real) is refused even when it is the one already kept. «Test the connection» opens a payment nobody pays; «Test payment» is paid with the trial system’s test card. The customer pays on the company’s own page, and the result comes back signed (HMAC-SHA512) both to the server and with the browser. Each result is checked, kept (a forged one keeps only a kilobyte), matched by the company’s signed order number rather than the unsigned reference, and acted on once whichever way it came, with a unique database rule as the last guard. The amount and currency are compared with what was asked, and only a plain sale counts as paid: a refund, void or authorisation never does. The results’ doors have their own rate limit and size cap at the gateway. The switch stays locked until the order’s own payment, the books and refunds are built.

reels.title: The shop’s own short videos, each with the products in it — published only by the owner
reels.text: Reels from the showroom, in the way people already watch them: one video a screen, swiped up for the next, silent until a tap, liked with a double tap. What is new is the shop around it: the product in the video pops up on the video at the second it shows, the products are listed under it with the shop’s own card and button, and a product’s page offers «see it in a video», opened at its second. The marketing team uploads from a phone (in 8 MB pieces, so a weak line resends one piece), a media worker with ffmpeg makes a light 720p copy and three covers on the shop’s own computer, and nothing reaches a customer until the owner approves it and turns the feature on. Views count once a phone a day, likes once a phone, and customers see the numbers from 100 views on.

documentsAppliedOnce.title: A purchase, a transfer and a stock hold are applied once — a double press no longer receives the goods twice
documentsAppliedOnce.text: A purchase order, a stock transfer and a stock hold carried nothing that said which version of them a request had read, so two requests on one document each applied it: a double press on «Receive» took the goods into stock twice and moved their average cost twice, a transfer arrived twice, a hold was deducted twice. Each of them, and each of their lines, now carries the database row’s own version: a request that worked from a copy read before another one saved is refused with «the record was changed, refresh», and nothing of it is kept — its stock, its lines and its booking events roll back together. A purchase draft saved twice keeps the lines of the save that won. Each case came with a test on a real PostgreSQL that failed first, was read by a reviewer from five directions, and was rehearsed on a copy of the stock database — every action pressed twice at the same instant took effect once — before going live.

reelsToFacebook.title: A reel goes to the shop’s Facebook Page with one press — as a real Facebook Reel
reelsToFacebook.text: A link pasted on Facebook shows only as a card; an uploaded reel plays. So the owner connects the shop’s Facebook Page once: he pastes the Page’s ID and its access token himself, the server seals the token the moment it arrives (AES-GCM, with a key derived from the services’ own secret) and never shows it again, and «Test the connection» asks Facebook whose token it is — it passes only for that Page. On any reel live on the site he presses «Publish to Facebook»: the words are drafted from the reel’s own title, products and link, he edits them, and a background worker carries Meta’s three steps (start, upload, finish), then reads the video’s status until Facebook publishes it or says why not. Each press carries its own id, so a repeated request is one post; the database allows one post in flight per reel; the publish call is marked before it goes and never sent twice; Facebook’s refusals come back in plain words. A dry run checks everything and sends nothing, and the switch arrives off.

backInStock.title: «Notify me when it is back» — the customer is told the moment stock arrives, off until the owner turns it on
backInStock.text: On a product that is out of stock, a customer leaves a name and a mobile (an email and his phone's notifications if he wants them). The stock service says by itself when a product goes from nothing to sell to some — it watches the save, so a receipt, a count, a return or a cancelled order all count — and puts that news on the message bus in the same save. The notification service then tells each waiting customer once, by email and a free phone notification, and gives the owner a list with a WhatsApp message ready for each; the program never sends WhatsApp itself. Rehearsed end to end on copies of the databases with a message bus of its own before it went live.

foundCheaper.title: «Found it cheaper?» — a customer tells the owner where they saw a product for less, off until the owner turns it on
foundCheaper.text: Under a product's price, a customer says where they saw it for less, at what price, with a link or a photo of it, and leaves a name and a mobile. The server reads the shop's own price from the catalogue — the price the page shows, never one sent from the form — and refuses a price that is not lower, a report without proof, a file that is not a picture, or too many from one mobile in a day. The report reaches the owner's list with both prices and the difference; the customer joins the shop's contacts and the owner answers on WhatsApp. Nothing in it changes a price. Rehearsed on a copy of its database before it went live.
